And he heard that the bishop was celebrating the feast of Hosannas (Palm Sunday) in one of his monasteries,
and he laid an ambush for him on the road.
And when the bishop set out on Monday of Passion Week to enter the city,
his son, who was also a great and renowned man, was with him.
He said to his father, the bishop:
"You go into the city,
and I wish to go and recreate myself in a certain village,
because they wish to consecrate a church that they have built."
And his father permitted him to go and not to delay.
And when they had parted from one another,
three Turkish horsemen came to meet the bishop,
and they dismounted and went and kissed his hand.
And they said to him:
"An envoy has come, and he summons you and also your son, to read a yarligh (decree) which he has with him."
And the bishop said:
"My son has gone to a certain village,
and behold, I am coming."
And when they had traveled a little way,
about two hundred Turkish horsemen fell upon them,
and they killed the bishop and thirty persons of the priests, monks, and other servants who were with him.
And they cut off his head,
and took it, and went and captured that village,
and they surrounded very vigilantly also the church in which the bishop's son was.
And when they entered the church,
they did not find him, because there was grass/straw there,
and inside it he was hidden.
And when they were about to leave,
one of those accursed oppressors said:
"First let us burn this grass/straw,
and then let us go."
And when he set fire to it,
that ill-fated man came out.
And the Turks said to him:
"Where is your father?" And he replied:
"He has gone into the city."
Then they cast his head before him.
And when he saw it,
he wailed and fell upon his father's head.
And as he thus fell,
they chopped him limb from limb.
And after these things, that wicked old man Bishara took his sons and all his servants,
and emigrated to the ruler of Egypt.
And the Parwana,
who was the regent of the kingdom of the Romans (Rūm),
fearing lest the Mongols suspect him
of also having his heart inclined toward the Egyptians,
arose and took the daughter of Sultan Rukn al-Din,
and brought her into the service of the King of Kings (Abaqa Khan).
